Read About Phnom Penh

A city that was founded by legend, built by a colonial power, emptied by its own countrymen in four days, and repopulated almost from zero — and that still somehow reads, today, as unhurried.

Four rivers and an old woman named Penh

Phnom Penh sits at Chaktomuk — the four faces — where the Tonle Sap, the Mekong and the Bassac cross in a wide X in front of what is now the Royal Palace. This confluence is the whole reason a city exists here at all, and the city's founding legend is built directly around it. In 1372, so the story goes, a wealthy widow named Penh was living on a mound near the riverbank when she saw a koki tree floating in the current after a flood. She had it pulled ashore, and inside it were four bronze Buddha statues and one statue of Vishnu. She had a hill built to house them — a phnom, the Khmer word for hill — and a small temple on top. That temple became Wat Phnom, and the city that grew up around the hill took its name from it: Phnom Penh, the hill of Penh.

The city did not become Cambodia's permanent capital immediately. Angkor had been abandoned as the royal seat by the 15th century, and the capital moved between several sites over the following centuries — Longvek, Oudong — before Phnom Penh was fixed as the seat of government in 1866, under King Norodom, three years into the French protectorate. The hill and its temple predate the capital by five hundred years; the city grew up around a piece of religious geography that was already old by the time it became a capital at all.

The French protectorate city

France established a protectorate over Cambodia in 1863 and governed it, alongside Vietnam and Laos, as part of French Indochina until 1953. The Phnom Penh a visitor walks through today — the wide boulevards, the grid street plan, the yellow-ochre colonial buildings — is substantially a French creation, laid down over the last third of the 19th century and the first half of the 20th. The Royal Palace itself, in its current form, was rebuilt starting in 1866 in Khmer style but with French engineering and, in places, French materials — the Napoleon III Pavilion inside the palace grounds is literally a cast-iron structure gifted by France, shipped from Paris and reassembled in Phnom Penh.

The civic buildings from this period are some of the best-preserved French colonial architecture in Southeast Asia, in part because Phnom Penh's 20th-century catastrophes emptied the city rather than bombing it flat. The Central Post Office, finished in 1895, the National Museum, opened in 1920 in ochre-red terracotta to house Angkorian-era sculpture pulled in from around the country, and the old railway station all date from this period. The French also laid out Sisowath Quay along the riverfront and the wide diagonal boulevards that still structure how the city reads on a map — a grid imposed on top of a settlement that had grown organically around a hill and a river confluence for five centuries before the French arrived.

Phnom Penh in the 1960s was known across Asia as the Pearl of the Orient — a glamorous, French-flavored capital of wide avenues, modernist architecture and a young, internationally minded elite. Almost none of the people who lived that decade are still in the city that resulted from what came next.

Independence, and the years before the war

Cambodia gained independence from France in 1953 under King Norodom Sihanouk, who abdicated the throne the following year to enter politics directly as head of state, a maneuver that let him dominate Cambodian politics for the next fifteen years. The period from independence to 1970 is remembered, especially in Phnom Penh, as something close to a golden age: the city modernized fast, a distinctive New Khmer Architecture movement (led by the architect Vann Molyvann, who designed the Independence Monument you'll pass on this itinerary) fused Angkorian forms with mid-century modernism, and the capital had a reputation across the region for style and ease. Sihanouk kept Cambodia formally neutral through the early years of the Vietnam War, a position that became harder to sustain as the war next door intensified.

That balance broke in 1970, when Sihanouk was deposed in a coup by his own prime minister, General Lon Nol, while abroad. Lon Nol aligned Cambodia with the United States and South Vietnam against the Vietnamese communists, and the country was drawn directly into the Vietnam War — American bombing of Cambodian territory, intended to disrupt North Vietnamese supply lines, intensified through the early 1970s and destabilized the countryside in ways that fed directly into what followed. The Cambodian Civil War, fought between Lon Nol's government and the Khmer Rouge insurgency, lasted five years and ended in Phnom Penh on April 17, 1975.

Year Zero

When Khmer Rouge forces entered Phnom Penh on April 17, 1975, the city held an estimated two million people, swollen by refugees fleeing the civil war in the countryside. Within days, the entire population was forced out on foot — the sick, the elderly, patients pulled from hospital beds with IV drips still attached — on the pretext of a temporary evacuation to avoid American bombing. It was not temporary. Phnom Penh became, for nearly four years, essentially an empty city: a small Khmer Rouge cadre population and almost no one else, while the deported urban population was put to forced agricultural labor in the countryside under an ideology that treated the very existence of cities, money, private property, religion and family structure as symptoms of a corrupt old order to be erased and rebuilt from "Year Zero."

What happened over the next three years and eight months killed an estimated one and a half to two million people — through execution, starvation, disease and forced labor — out of a national population of roughly eight million. Tuol Sleng, a former high school converted into the S-21 interrogation and torture center, and Choeung Ek, one of the killing sites where S-21's prisoners were executed, are both on this itinerary's second day, and both are run today as memorial museums rather than softened into anything else. Phnom Penh is one of very few national capitals in the modern world that was, within living memory, deliberately and almost completely emptied of people by its own government.

Vietnamese forces captured Phnom Penh on January 7, 1979, ending Khmer Rouge rule. The city they entered was close to a ghost town — weeds through the pavement, empty apartment blocks, a capital that had to be resettled almost from scratch.

What came back

Resettlement began in 1979 and was slow and improvised — people returning from the countryside to a city with damaged infrastructure, no functioning currency (money itself had been abolished by the Khmer Rouge), and, in the earliest years, chronic food shortages. The 1980s were still difficult: Cambodia was under a Vietnamese-backed government not recognized by much of the international community, and the Khmer Rouge continued an insurgency from border areas for another two decades. The turning point was the UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC), which administered a transition to internationally supervised elections in 1993 and helped restore the monarchy, with Norodom Sihanouk returning as king.

Rebuilding a capital's population, economy and institutions from close to zero is not something that happens on any predictable timeline, and Phnom Penh's recovery has been genuinely uneven — decades of it were consumed just by re-establishing basic civic and religious life. The wats you'll visit on this itinerary, including ones founded in the 15th century, were almost all rebuilt and restaffed after 1979 rather than continuously operating across the centuries their founding dates imply; nearly the entire monkhood had been killed or forcibly disrobed under the Khmer Rouge. What looks, on a stop-by-stop basis, like centuries of continuous tradition is, underneath, largely a single generation's work of reconstruction.

The city now

The Phnom Penh a visitor sees today is the product of a genuinely fast build-out concentrated in the last twenty-five years or so: garment manufacturing and, more recently, Chinese investment and tourism have driven rapid construction, and the skyline along the Bassac and around Koh Pich — the reclaimed sandbar island you'll pass on Day 3 — is almost entirely 21st-century. That new skyline sits directly against the French-era grid and the Angkorian-legacy temples, often on the same block, which is part of what makes the city visually specific: colonial shophouses, glass towers, saffron-robed monks and orange tuk-tuks share the same short stretch of street without much friction.

Demographically, this is a young country living around an old wound. More than half of Cambodia's population was born after the Khmer Rouge period ended, and the country's median age is among the lowest in Asia — a society that is, on the street level, youthful, informal and forward-looking, built on top of a still-living memory of catastrophe that the older generation carries directly and the younger generation inherits through family, museums and a national school curriculum that now, finally, teaches the period in detail.

The thing to carry

Before you set out, here is what reframes the whole itinerary: almost nothing you're about to see is as old as it looks. The Royal Palace, the wats, the colonial boulevards — all of it reads as continuous heritage, and none of it quite is. The city was founded on a legend about a hill and a floating tree, built out by a colonial administration that lasted ninety years, emptied by its own government for nearly four, and then rebuilt, block by block and temple by temple, by a population that had to reconstruct civic life from very close to nothing. Phnom Penh's calm today — the riverside cafés, the unhurried pace along Sisowath Quay — isn't the absence of a difficult history. It's what forty-five years of deliberate rebuilding on top of that history looks like when it's still, visibly, in progress.
